tier_reason: Upgraded from D. The README chart has no numbers, but Speedb's own docs page for the sorted hash memtable gives numeric headline gains over RocksDB v7.2.2 (default skiplist memtable) with a db_bench configuration. It is first-party, gives only a core count and no CPU model, compiler or flags, and states the numbers as 'up to' figures, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Speedb's sorted hash memtable vs RocksDB v7.2.2 with its skiplist memtable: "Up to 155% improvement in overwrite workload", "Up to 68% improvement in 50% random read workload", "Up to 15% improvement in random seek workload". Per-point values are only in chart images. The README and dynamic-delayed-writes doc only show a chart (no numbers) of steady random-write throughput without stalls vs RocksDB's older delayed-write mechanism.
corrections.workload: db_bench with 1 billion objects, 1KB values, 64MB write buffer, 4 threads, max 4 write buffers, 1 column family, 16 CPU cores, no compression: 100% overwrite, 50% random read, and 100% random seek, comparing Speedb with the sorted hash memtable (speedb.HashSpdRepFactory) against RocksDB v7.2.2 with its default skiplist memtable.
corrections.hardware: Memtable test: 16 CPU cores, model not stated. Delayed-write test in the README: 16 cores of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C @ 2.80GHz (per the dynamic-delayed-writes doc).
corrections.caveats: First-party vendor docs, and the figures are 'up to' headlines; per-point results exist only as chart images. The sorted hash memtable is opt-in (--memtablerep=speedb.HashSpdRepFactory), not the default. The baseline is old: RocksDB v7.2.2. No compiler, flags or CPU model are given for the memtable test. The README's delayed-write chart has no numbers. docs.speedb.io no longer resolves; the docs survive in the speedb-io/documentation GitHub repo. Commits stopped in March 2024, the same month as an HN-listed TechCrunch story (2024-03-21) that says Redis acquired Speedb.

notes: benchmark_url now points to the docs page that has actual numbers vs RocksDB; the README anchor is chart-only. Metadata matches gh: Apache-2.0, 1009 stars, last commit 2024-03-11 (stale), not archived and not a fork. The paired-bloom-filter doc makes a memory claim (about 30% less memory at equal FPR) but says construction and use are about 2x slower, so it is not a speed win.

tier_reason: OSDI'20 peer-reviewed paper; every result compares Bourbon only against WiscKey, the authors' LevelDB-derived key-value-separated LSM, not against stock LevelDB or RocksDB. The CPU (Xeon E5-2660) and code (read_cold, scripts/run_*.sh; CMake RELEASE build) are available, but the compiler and its version are never stated, so it is not A.

corrections.baseline: WiscKey (the authors' LevelDB-derived LSM with key-value separation; no direct stock-LevelDB or RocksDB comparison)
corrections.workload: Read-only lookups (10M operations, 16B integer keys, 64B values, in-memory) on six datasets (linear, seg-1%, seg-10%, normal with 64M keys; Amazon Reviews 33.5M; NY OpenStreetMaps 21.9M), comparing Bourbon's per-file greedy piecewise-linear-regression models (error bound 8) with the WiscKey baseline; plus YCSB, SOSD, Optane SSD and limited-memory runs.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: "BOURBON improves lookup performance by 1.23x-1.78x as compared to state-of-the-art production LSMs". In Fig. 9 the baseline is WiscKey, with 1.23x-1.78x lower average lookup latency across six datasets. vs WiscKey elsewhere: YCSB-C about 1.6x, YCSB-B/D 1.24x-1.44x, YCSB-A/F 1.06x-1.18x, YCSB-E 1.16x-1.19x; SOSD 1.48x-1.74x; Optane SSD 1.25x-1.28x; SATA SSD with limited memory 1.04x (uniform) and 1.25x (zipfian).
corrections.hardware: 20-core Intel Xeon CPU E5-2660, 160 GB memory, 480 GB SATA SSD (CloudLab c220g2 per ARTIFACT_README); the fast-storage runs used an Intel Optane SSD.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated; built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE -DNDEBUG_SWITCH=ON (ARTIFACT_README/CS736_README)
corrections.caveats: The only baseline is WiscKey (a research LSM built on LevelDB), despite the abstract's 'production LSMs' wording; there is no RocksDB or stock-LevelDB head-to-head. Gains are for lookups only, with integer keys; string keys and key compression are unsupported, and writes are not improved. This GitHub repo is not the authors' own: a third party (Edward Fang) imported it as a snapshot ('original bourbon', 2020-10-11) of the authors' Bitbucket learned-leveldb artifact. It then added CS736 course-project changes (offline/synchronous level learning, 'mode 9') and a 2023 PLR NaN-slope fix. The README says the owner is not the paper's author. Compiler is unstated.

notes: The 1.23x-1.78x quote is verbatim from the USENIX abstract and paper. The record's baseline ('LevelDB / production LSM (RocksDB-class)') and workload ('unmodified production LSM implementations') overstate it, because the paper measures only against WiscKey. Kept at B, not rejected, since WiscKey is a recognizable LevelDB derivative. The authors' original code is public at bitbucket.org/daiyifandanny/learned-leveldb (Bitbucket API: public, last updated 2020-10-05); consider re-pointing the entry there. gh metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 47 stars, last commit 2023-09-06 (abandoned, just over 3 years old).

tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The SOSP'21 paper (Sec. 6.1) states the Intel Xeon Gold 6132 and GCC 7.5.0. Flags are set in public Makefiles: cuckoo-trie-code/Makefile (-O3 -fvisibility=hidden -flto -fno-strict-aliasing -march=haswell) and the baselines' in cuckoo-trie/other-benchmarked-indexes (stx, hot: -O3 -march=native; artolc: -O3; wormhole driver: -O2). Benchmark code is public: benchmark.c plus stx/test_stx.cpp, hot, artolc/test_artolc.cpp, wormhole/test_wormhole.c.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.5.0 (paper). Cuckoo Trie: -O3 -fvisibility=hidden -flto -fno-strict-aliasing -march=haswell -DNDEBUG (Makefile). Baselines in other-benchmarked-indexes: STX and HOT -O3 -march=native, ARTOLC -O3, Wormhole driver -O2.
corrections.caveats: Research code: the README says it 'was created to run the experiments in the paper' and 'is not robust enough to be used as an index in your program'. It runs on Linux x86_64 only and needs 2MB huge pages plus a huge-page allocator (jemalloc, THP) for paper-level numbers. The Cuckoo Trie is slower on the az dataset (long common prefixes), on scan-heavy YCSB-E, and on inserts vs ARTOLC. The 360% win is over the STX B+-tree (tlx), not std::map. Optimization flags differ slightly across the compared indexes. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant. The baselines' benchmark repo (other-benchmarked-indexes) has no license.

notes: The quote is verbatim from the SOSP'21 paper (arXiv 2201.09331, Sec. 6.2); the abstract gives the 20%-360% range. The last default-branch commit is 2021-10-23 ('Add short summary and full paper citation to readme'). gh's pushed_at of 2024-05-14 is not a commit on main, so maintenance moves from stale to abandoned.
